If SAF production significantly increases, there would be potential to deliver SAF and Jet A separately by barge or tanker to New England terminals for blending and delivery to airports. Shell’s Providence terminal can receive fuel by unit-car train. If SAF were produced in the Midwest, it could be delivered by rail to Providence, where it could be offloaded to trucks or barges/tankers with additional equipment. There is potential to evaluate existing but unused rail at other terminals. While fuels deliveries by rail are limited in New England, Massport receives renewable diesel that is delivered by rail to Broco Energy—while they do not handle jet fuel at any of their facilities, it could be considered. SAF Produced in New England NLR contacted all terminal companies in the region to discuss their fuel receiving and offloading modes and their potential to accommodate SAF, Jet A, and associated blending infrastructure. Movements, storage, and blending of SAF produced in New England requires more consideration compared with receipt of a SAF/Jet A blend from New York Harbor. A SAF biorefinery is not expected along the coast due to the high value of land. Therefore, local SAF production is expected to be delivered to terminals by truck or barge. The Energy Transfer terminal, which supplies the highest volume of Jet A in the region, cannot receive fuel by truck, only by barge, and space for additional tanks and associated infrastructure is limited. Therefore, other terminals were evaluated for their potential to handle locally produced SAF. A preferred terminal for blending SAF produced in New England would have the following attributes to reduce costs: • Located near a SAF production facility. • Currently stores jet fuel due to existing dedicated infrastructure to reduce capital costs. • Existing infrastructure to receive fuel by truck. • Existing infrastructure to offload fuel by both truck and marine. It is generally preferred to blend SAF at terminals already storing jet fuel, as there is dedicated infrastructure, and the investment would generally be lower than adding jet fuel to a terminal not currently handling it. A SAF plant located near a terminal would benefit from lower trucking costs. Sprague Energy’s South Portland, Maine, and Quincy, Massachusetts, terminals both meet these criteria. Currently, the Quincy location stores jet fuel solely for military use. The primary consideration for offloading by ship is for delivery to Energy Transfer’s East Boston terminal for delivery to BOS—the airport with the highest Jet A consumption.
